newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian protests persist after pyramid collapse.
newsitem.headline: Albanian protests persist after pyramid collapse.

text.p: Anti-government protests and a student hunger strike over fraudulent investment schemes which ruined thousands of Albanians showed no sign of abating on Sunday.
About 5,000 anti-government marchers staged a boisterous march in the southern port of Vlore for a 19th day to demand the government quit over its handling of the scandal.
The south has been particularly hard hit by the collapse of five pyramid schemes in January which wiped out the savings of hundreds of thousands of people across the country.
Investors blame the right-wing government of President Sali Berisha and Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi for failing to regulate the schemes and to warn the public of their dangers.
"How can the government which was in power during the theft be trusted to make sure the money is returned?" asked protester Engjell Dine. "We're determined to keep going."

The region around Vlore invested heavily in the Gjallica fund, which owes some $363 million to duped investors. The couple who ran the fund have fled Albania but they have been charged with fraud along with 20 other defendants.
The demonstrators rallied in front of Vlore university to express support for 53 students inside who have been on hunger strike since Thursday.
"All of our families invested in Gjallica and they lost all their savings. It has affected the lives of everyone in Vlore," student leader Leonard Kajtalli told Reuters.
He said the students were determined to press their hunger strike until the government resigned and a technical government was set up to sort out the pyramid mess.
Officials estimate $1 to $2 billion could have been lost in the schemes, which used cash from new investors to pay interest as high as 60 percent a month to earlier investors.
After the get-rich-quick pyramids collapsed, Albania was swept by protests and riots. Clashes between protesters and riot police erupted again last Thursday in Tirana.
The ruling Democrats have been struggling to regain support, with ministers fanning out across the country to admit mistakes and promise economic measures to help investors.

But the government has said repeatedly that no state funds will be used to reimburse losses. Berisha has told hapless investors bluntly that they had learned a hard lesson from the country's recent embrace of capitalism.

For 45 years Albania was one of the world's most ruthlessly controlled and isolated communist states. Single-party rule was pushed aside in 1990 and thousands of destitute Albanians fled the Balkan country to seek work overseas.
Much of the money which the illegal immigrants sent home to their families was invested in the pyramids and diplomats fear the collapse could spark a new wave of emigration.
In Tirana, the Democratic Party agreed on Saturday to choose their candidate for president during the coming week -- Berisha is certain to be selected for a second term.
Under the constitution, Berisha's powers have been limited ahead of the vote in parliament in March for the president. His party has an absolute majority.

The opposition has said it will not rest until Berisha and Meksi resign but for the moment that looks unlikely. Deputy Prime Minister Tritan Shehu told Reuters on Saturday there was no question of Meksi resigning at the moment.
